title: Fetal Effects of Autoimmune Disease

paragraphs.text: 19 Fetal Effects of Autoimmune Disease
paragraphs.heading: Overview

paragraphs.text: The maternal-fetal interface is quite efficient in its selective exclusion of substances during the transport process from the maternal to the fetal circulation. At the same time, the placenta selectively transfers other substances, a process that is facilitated by the proximity of the respective maternal-fetal vascular systems within the placental cotyledons. Although there is no mixing of the maternal and fetal blood, the placental barrier is not impermeable, and small amounts of fetal blood, including fetal cells, gain access to the maternal circulation in most pregnancies through breaks in the fetal-maternal interface. When fetal blood cells are recognized as antigens by the maternal immunologic system, they may provoke an immune response and the production of immunoglobulins. This mechanism occurs in only a few pregnancies and is the basis of incompatibility disorders (see Chapter 22), whereby exogenous antigens such as fetal cells or incompatible blood sensitize the maternal immune system. The maternal antibodies, which are produced as a response to sensitization, cross the placenta and may destroy fetal cells.1,2 Generally, the mother is disease free, and the diagnosis is reached usually after the delivery of an affected infant and in some cases by sonographic findings.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Transfer: General Remarks

paragraphs.text: A second type of maternal antibody that crosses the placenta and affects the fetus may arise from sensitization of the mother’s immune system by her endogenous antigens, with the resultant production of autoantibodies. The mother with autoantibodies has an autoimmune disorder, and the diagnosis of the maternal disease usually precedes the diagnosis of the fetal or neonatal complication.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Transfer: General Remarks

paragraphs.text: These generalizations describe immune processes that may affect the fetus or neonate. Although the maternal immune system may produce a wide range of immunoglobulins, only maternal antibodies of the immunoglobulin G (IgG) class (but not IgM or IgA) can cross the placental barrier. The common denominators of such disorders are the production of IgG in the maternal compartment, the transfer of IgG through the placenta, and the effects of these
paragraphs.heading: Placental Transfer: General Remarks

paragraphs.text: antibodies in the fetal compartment or neonate. Maternal IgG antibodies are also transferred to the newborns through breast feeding and may cause autoimmunity pathologies.3–5 This chapter discusses examples of such disorders.
paragraphs.heading: Placental Transfer: General Remarks

paragraphs.text: Box 19.1 lists the immunologic etiologies of fetal and consequently neonatal thrombocytopenia. The most significant pathologies are neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Although the two conditions have some similarities, they are distinct diseases, each with a different underlying pathogenesis (Table 19.1) (see Chapter 80).
paragraphs.heading: Fetal Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: ITP in adults is often a chronic disease mediated by autoantibodies directed against cell surface components (glycoproteins) of platelets (IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX). Thrombocytopenia occurs when the platelet-antibody complexes are destroyed by the reticuloendothelial system. A low platelet count raises suspicion for ITP, but the diagnosis is reached after exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia by history, physical examination, blood count, peripheral blood smear, and autoimmune profile.6–8 A spuriously low platelet count should be evaluated by examining a blood smear to exclude
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: pseudothrombocytopenia caused by ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA)-dependent platelet agglutination. The normal range of platelet counts in nonpregnant women and neonates is 150,000 to 400,000/μL; however, the mean counts tend to be lower during pregnancy. The prevalence of maternal ITP is one to two cases per 1000 deliveries; the prevalence of fetal or neonatal ITP is lower.9 The potential risk of a low platelet count for the mother is bleeding; however, the risk becomes significant only when the platelet count becomes less than 20,000/μL. A maternal platelet count of greater than 50,000/μL is considered to be hemostatic during vaginal or cesarean birth.
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: Thrombocytopenia of the fetus or newborn is caused by active transplacental transport of the antiplatelet antibodies; however, no significant correlation has been observed between neonatal thrombocytopenia and maternal autoimmune antibodies or platelet count. The concern is for the potential trauma at birth and the potential risk for cerebral hemorrhage in the neonate. In the past, obstetricians performed antepartum cordocentesis (percutaneous umbilical vein blood sampling [PUBS]) or fetal scalp blood sampling to identify a fetus with a platelet count less than 50,000/μL and to deliver the fetus by the abdominal route. A recent meta-analysis revealed a prevalence of 24% for neonatal thrombocytopenia in cases of maternal ITP; however, hemorrhage was only reported in 4.1% of the observed neonatal thrombocytopenia cases. The rarity of fetal or neonatal consequences of maternal ITP does not justify a routine intrauterine platelet evaluation for those fetuses.9,11 The current view holds that PUBS and fetal scalp sampling are not recommended, as there is a risk of hemorrhage and fetal loss comparable to nonintervention. Generally, cesarean delivery is reserved for obstetric indications. ITP often worsens during the course of pregnancy, with only 5.6% of women with ITP showing improvement in platelet count during pregnancy.
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: There are specific guidelines for following and treating ITP during pregnancy.12,13 Pregnant patients with ITP and platelet counts greater than 50,000/μL throughout gestation and patients with platelet counts of 30,000 to 50,000/μL in the first or second trimester do not routinely require treatment. Treatment in the form of glucocorticoids
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) is indicated in patients with platelet counts less than 10,000/μL and patients with platelet counts of 10,000 to 30,000/μL who are in their second or third trimester or are bleeding. When glucocorticoid and IVIG therapy have failed, splenectomy is appropriate in the second trimester in women with platelet counts less than 10,000/μL who are bleeding. Splenectomy should not be performed in asymptomatic pregnant women with platelet counts greater than 10,000/μL. Platelet transfusion is indicated for patients with counts less than 10,000/μL before a planned cesarean section and for those who are bleeding and expected to deliver vaginally. Prophylactic transfusions are unnecessary when the platelet count is greater than 30,000/μL and there is no bleeding.
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: ITP does not preclude breastfeeding. The use of IVIG during pregnancy may improve platelet counts in the mother, but the treatment may not prevent fetal thrombocytopenia because the placental transfer of IVIG is inconsistent and mostly insufficient to reach fetal therapeutic levels.14 A retrospective study examined the morbidity of 92 obstetric patients with ITP during 119 pregnancies over an 11-year period.15 The authors found that most of these patients had thrombocytopenia during pregnancy. At delivery, 89% had platelet counts less than 150,000/μL. For many patients, the pregnancy was uneventful; however, 21.5% of the women had moderate to severe bleeding. In 31.1% of the pregnancies, treatment was required to increase the platelet counts. Most deliveries (82.4%) were vaginal. Platelet counts of less than 150,000/μL were found in 25.2% of the infants, including 9% with platelet counts less than 50,000/μL. Treatment for hemostatic impairment was necessary in 14.6% of the infants. During the study period, two fetal deaths occurred, including one caused by hemorrhage.15
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: After birth, the platelet count of newborns whose mothers have ITP-mediated thrombocytopenia may continue to decrease, and careful follow-up of the thrombocytopenia should be performed during the first week of life. Less than 1% of neonates develop intracranial hemorrhage (ICH). Ultrasound imaging of the brain seems to be indicated if the count is less than 50,000/μL, even in the absence of neurologic findings. Neonates who exhibit severe thrombocytopenia
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: (<20,000–30,000/μL) should be treated with platelet transfusion or IVIG, or both. Neonates with ICH or any other bleeding manifestation should be treated with combined platelet transfusion and IVIG or glucocorticoid therapy when the platelet count is less than 100,000/μL. Neonatal thrombocytopenia usually resolves within 4 to 6 weeks.
paragraphs.heading: Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

paragraphs.text: Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) is a rare but serious condition associated with significant fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. The pathogenesis is similar to Rh disease. A mother with antigen-negative platelets is sensitized by antigen-positive fetal platelets gaining access to the maternal circulation via breaches in the placental barrier. As a result, the mother produces antiplatelet antibodies, and these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the fetal platelets. In contrast to Rh disease, 50% of FNAIT cases occur during the first pregnancy of couples at risk. This difference is explained by the higher immunogenicity of the platelet antigen and the smaller size of the platelets, which may facilitate their fetomaternal transfusion.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: Of the several types of platelet antigens, the human platelet antigen 1a (HPA-1a) is involved in 80% to 90% of FNAIT cases among Caucasians, and HPA-5b is responsible for a further 5% to 15% of the cases. Among people of color (e.g., Asians), HPA-1a incompatibility is a rare cause of FNAIT, and other alloantigens (e.g., HPA-4b) are implicated. The fetus acquires the antigen from the father. When the father is heterozygous, 50% of the fetuses would be affected, whereas all fetuses of a homozygous father would be HPA positive.16,17 The prevalence of FNAIT is 1 case per 1000 deliveries. Fetomaternal platelet incompatibility is much more frequent. The discrepancy is explained by the facilitating role of certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types that are associated with the development of FNAIT. HLA-DR3 is associated with a 10- to 30-fold risk for HPA- 1a antibody production.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: In the usual scenario, an asymptomatic woman delivers an otherwise normal infant in an otherwise uncomplicated birth. Most neonates are asymptomatic, and the thrombocytopenia is detected by a blood count performed for other perinatal causes. In some cases, neonates present with generalized petechiae, hemorrhage into abdominal viscera, excessive bleeding after venipuncture or circumcision, or, in extreme cases, abnormal neurologic manifestations secondary to ICH. The platelet count commonly decreases further during the first week after birth. Less common presentation is an intrauterine sonographic diagnosis of fetal ICH, found to be secondary to fetal thrombocytopenia caused by FNAIT.18,19
paragraphs.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis of FNAIT involves typing platelet antigens in the newborn and in the parents to show that the mother lacks a platelet antigen that is present on the platelets of the father and the neonate. A more sophisticated test is to establish the existence of the antiplatelet antibody in the mother’s serum that is directed against a platelet antigen in
paragraphs.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: the father. Testing the infant is generally unnecessary if the father is available for testing. HPA genotyping is available as a routine laboratory technique and can be used to identify HPA incompatibilities between mother and child. Universal screening is not recommended by any professional organization due to the low prevalence of FNAIT. However, it is possible to accurately screen for HPA-1a, which causes 75% of FNAIT cases.20–22
paragraphs.heading: Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

paragraphs.text: In suspected cases of FNAIT, treatment should be started on the basis of the clinical diagnosis without waiting for the results of the immunologic workup. Management depends on the gestational age of the infant, the severity of the thrombocytopenia, the presence of bleeding, and the presence of additional risk factors for bleeding. Treatment is based on transfusion of random-donor, ABO-compatible and Rh-compatible, and HPA-1a-negative platelets (preferably with HPA-5b-negative platelets, as well) in neonates with severe thrombocytopenia. This transfusion is compatible in approximately 90% of cases of FNAIT.22 When random-donor platelets are unavailable, washed maternal platelets can be administered. HPA-incompatible platelets should be used only if compatible ones are unavailable; they can be combined with IVIG treatment to achieve a transient increase in the platelet count until IVIG becomes effective.20
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: High-dose IVIG, 1 g/kg per day for 2 days or 0.5 g/kg per day for 4 days, is also effective in increasing the platelet count in most cases, although the increase may be delayed for 1 or 2 days.9 Corticosteroids were used in the past but have become less popular since the availability of IVIG. In any case, the neonatal platelet count should be closely monitored during the first days of life.
paragraphs.heading: Management of the Neonate

paragraphs.text: When the diagnosis of alloimmune thrombocytopenia is established, parents should be counseled regarding risks and management of future pregnancies. The recurrence rate of FNAIT in a subsequent pregnancy is greater than 90%, and the risk for ICH is the same or greater than in the previous pregnancy. There are conflicting data regarding increased severity of FNAIT in subsequent pregnancies.23
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: HPA-1a alloimmunization tends to cause a more significant disease compared to other antibodies. Low and stable maternal levels of HPA-1a during the pregnancy are correlated with a low risk of FNAIT development.24 Fetal ICH in previous pregnancies increase the risk of recurrence, which tends to be in earlier gestational weeks. Administration of IVIG therapy during the pregnancy is considered protective against FNAIT.
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: The risk for antenatal ICH in the fetus with alloimmune thrombocytopenia is substantial enough to warrant intervention by giving the mother weekly infusions of high-dose IVIG with or without corticosteroids. Antenatal therapy is aimed at increasing the number of fetal platelets regardless of the presence of a risk factor.
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Although screening procedures are not indicated to detect FNAIT, a high index of suspicion is needed in certain cases (Box 19.2). Typically, a woman presents in early pregnancy with a history of delivering an infant with neonatal thrombocytopenia or presents with some clues to the diagnosis. The first step should be assessment of the father and the presence of incompatibility for the HPA antigen system between the parents. Antigens are tested according to the local laboratory protocols based on geographically and ethnic probabilities: HPA-1a/1b, HPA-3a/3b, HPA-4a/4b, HPA-5a/5b, HPA- 6a/6b, HPA-9a/9b, and HPA-15a/15b may be checked. If the father is heterozygous, the status of the fetus is unknown. In some places, a noninvasive evaluation of fetal typing through maternal blood is available. Direct assessment of fetal platelets via PUBS or via genotyping cells in the amniotic fluid may be performed. The timing of the procedure and the risk involved are matters of debate. Failure to treat carries the risk for intrauterine ICH, which is expected to occur in 30% of cases, with 10% of affected newborns dying and 20% experiencing neurologic sequelae secondary to ICH. PUBS has a high risk for miscarriage or fetal death. The operator must be prepared to transfuse platelets if the results show a dangerously low platelet count. If the infant is found to be HPA positive or the father is homozygous for the allele, there is a choice between serial platelet transfusions and IVIG administered to the mother. Amniocentesis is performed mainly to exclude the presence of platelet antigens and thus to avoid unnecessary interventions.25-27
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Serial intrauterine platelet transfusions carry the risk of a single PUBS multiplied by the number of procedures. Because the survival of transfused thrombocytes is short, performing serial intrauterine transfusions requires repeating the procedure every week or 10 days. In a study of the fetal loss rate in FNAIT managed by serial platelet transfusions, the authors found two perinatal losses in 12 pregnancies managed by a total of 84 platelet transfusions. One loss was procedure related and resulted from exsanguination despite platelet transfusion. The procedure-related fetal loss rate was 1.2% per procedure but 8.3% per pregnancy. The authors calculated a cumulative risk for serial weekly transfusions of approximately 6% per pregnancy, indicating the need to develop less invasive approaches.28
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: The invasive procedure is used less often now than previously; this may be the result of favorable outcomes related to maternal
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: treatment with high-dose IVIG (1 g/kg/wk). The beneficial effect of megadose IVIG is presumably mediated by masking the antigenic effect of fetal platelets, reducing the production of antiplatelet antibodies. IVIG also stabilizes endothelial cells and reduces the incidence of ICH even when the fetal platelet count remains low. It is debatable whether corticosteroids should be added to the IVIG management protocol.20,21,29
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: A European collaborative study of the antenatal management of FNAIT attempted to determine whether the severity of the disease in the current pregnancy could be predicted from the history of FNAIT in previous pregnancies and to assess the effects of different types of antenatal intervention. The study enrolled 56 women who had had a prior infant affected by FNAIT due to HPA-1a alloimmunization. The authors found that fetuses with a sibling history of antenatal ICH or severe thrombocytopenia (a platelet count of <20,000/μL) had significantly lower pretreatment platelet counts than fetuses whose siblings had less severe thrombocytopenia or postnatal ICH. Maternal therapy resulted in a platelet count exceeding 50,000/μL in 67% of cases. None of the fetuses managed by serial platelet intrauterine transfusions had ICH after treatment. Several serious complications of PUBS arose, however. The results of this study suggest that the start of therapy can be stratified on the basis of the sibling history of FNAIT and support the use of maternal therapy as first-line treatment.10
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Some patients who receive IVIG do not respond. Nonresponders cannot be recognized without PUBS, however. When PUBS is planned to assess the effectiveness of therapy, the preparation for intrauterine platelet transfusion should be similar to the procedure used when PUBS is performed to diagnose FNAIT in a case with a heterozygous father (i.e., when the risk of an affected fetus is 50%). Nonresponders may be treated with either serial intrauterine platelet transfusions or steroids added to IVIG. It has been suggested that such assessment of treatment is unnecessary in patients who previously responded to IVIG therapy.
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Alloimmune thrombocytopenia may also result from fetomaternal HLA mismatch. The meaning and treatment of this rare situation are controversial.
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Most patients are delivered by a term planned cesarean delivery. For patients who desire a vaginal delivery, a fetal platelet count is suggested for safety evaluation of a vaginal delivery. For patients with prior pregnancies with FNAIT, avoiding an affected fetus may be achieved by preimplantation genetic testing and an in vitro fertilization.21,30
paragraphs.heading: Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

paragraphs.text: Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are produced in various diseases with an immune component (Box 19.3). ANAs of the IgG and IgM types bind to nuclei or to nuclear components. Their presence is detected in the patient’s serum, and they may be classified according to their subunits, each of which is related to the diagnosis of a disease.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus. In this chapter, the maternal manifestations of these autoimmune diseases are not discussed; the focus is on neonatal lupus—a model of passively acquired autoimmunity—and the effects of the ANAs anti-Ro and anti-La.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Neonatal lupus is caused by transplacental passage of maternal autoantibodies. It is rare, as only about 1% of infants with maternal ANAs develop neonatal lupus. The infant may present with cardiac, dermatologic, hepatic, and hematologic manifestations. In children with neonatal lupus, there is commonly involvement of only one or two organ systems. The skin lesions on the face and scalp, often in a distinctive periorbital distribution, may be present at birth but usually develop within the first few weeks of life and tend to resolve in a few weeks or months without scarring.31 Fetal heart block typically begins during the second or third trimester of pregnancy. In some instances, this begins as first- or second-degree heart block and progresses to third-degree heart block. Complete heart block seems to be irreversible and may be combined with cardiomyopathy (see Chapter 78). Hepatobiliary complications (10% of cases) may be manifested as liver failure occurring at birth or in utero, transient conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, or transient transaminase elevations occurring in infancy. Thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or anemia occurs in about 10% of affected infants. The noncardiac manifestations are transient and tend to resolve within months after birth. A case of neonatal lupus affecting both twins has been described.32
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Mothers of children with neonatal lupus may have ANA-related connective tissue disease (e.g., systemic lupus
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, undifferentiated autoimmune syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis). The recurrence rate of neonatal lupus for a mother with anti-Ro autoantibodies, which are present in almost 95% of patients, is approximately 25%. IgG autoantibodies are found alone or in combination and are directed against Ro (SSA), La (SSB), or U1-RNA (U1-RNP) antigens, and their presence increases the risk for neonatal lupus erythematosus.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Anti-Ro and anti-La autoantibodies recognize cardiac adrenoceptors and muscarinic receptors, and this recognition may explain the cardiac arrhythmia associated with these ANAs. Maternal anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and complement components are deposited in fetal heart tissues, leading to inflammation, calcification, necrosis, and fibrosis of the conducting tissue (and, in some cases, of the surrounding myocardium).33 The postinflammation fibrotic response to injury is quite rapid and, in most cases, irreversible. The process by which maternal anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies begin and propagate inflammation that leads to scarring of the atrioventricular node is not entirely clear. It has been proposed that the process begins with apoptosis of cardiocytes, resulting in translocation of Ro or La antigens and subsequent surface binding by maternal ANAs. This leads to a phagocytosis-mediated scarring process.33 In addition, the anti-Ro antibodies have been shown to have arrhythmogenic activity through inhibition of calcium flux across cell membranes.34 Animal models suggest that reactivity to the p200 region of the Ro52 protein and antibody targeting of L-type calcium channels may be associated in the developing cardiac neonatal lupus.35 In vitro, the β2-glycoprotein I seems to prevent anti-Ro binding to apoptotic cells, the urokinase-plasminogen activator/receptor system seems to activate transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), and endothelin-1 secretion by macrophages seems to mediate tissue injury.35 It also appears that fetal major histocompatibility complex is involved in the pathogenesis.35 Interestingly, it was demonstrated that mothers of children with neonatal lupus accumulate genetic risk factors preferentially from the neonatal lupus child’s grandparents.35
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: The cardiac rhythm disorders increase the risk for fetal congestive heart failure and point to the most important intervention during pregnancy: close follow-up with echocardiography and ultrasonography. Echocardiography can show the conduction defect and estimate the cardiac function.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: About 10% of fetuses with congenital heart block are born with hydrops fetalis and congestive heart failure, and their prognosis is poor (see Chapter 22). Retrospective studies addressed the role of fluorinated steroids, IVIG, and hydroxychloroquine for prevention and treatment.35 Intrauterine treatment with maternal corticosteroids may decrease the pericardial effusion or improve the symptoms of heart failure. If first- or second-degree heart block is detected, oral dexamethasone, 4 mg daily, is recommended. The treatment is controversial because some of those blocks may resolve spontaneously, and dexamethasone treatment crosses placentas and may cause abortion, oligohydramnios, and abnormal fetal growth along with either maternal
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: hypertension and diabetes. Therefore it is sometimes recommended to treat only patients with fetuses that develop second-degree blocks. When complete heart block develops, the treatment is not effective anymore. IVIGs have not proven beneficial. Some data support hydrochloroquines as effective for patients with a previous pregnancy complicated with complete block. Most neonates born with a heart block secondary to neonatal lupus require pacemaker placement in the neonatal period or later in life.36,37
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antinuclear Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Phospholipids are involved in facilitating the coagulation cascade. Antiphospholipid antibodies (APLAs) are autoantibodies against phospholipids or against plasma proteins bound to phospholipids. The most common subgroups involved in disease states are anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant antibodies, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies. The hypercoagulability function of these antibodies is epitomized by the fact that they cause “bleeding in the test tube but clotting in the body,” referring to their involvement in pathologic clotting. APLAs promote clotting in arteries and veins (i.e., thrombophilia) by activation of endothelial cells, via oxidantmediated injury to endothelium, and by modulating the regulatory function of coagulation proteins.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

paragraphs.text: It is common practice to use clinical and laboratory criteria for the diagnosis of APLA syndrome. According to the Sapporo criteria, patients are required to have either vascular thrombosis (venous or arterial, including neurologic disease) or fetal loss and to show evidence of APLA either by the detection of anticardiolipin antibodies or by a positive test for lupus anticoagulant antibodies. At present, one should look for lupus anticoagulant, APLA, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I. To differentiate between persistent autoantibody response and transient responses from other causes, APLA must be detected on at least two occasions 12 weeks apart. These classification criteria are reported to have a sensitivity of greater than 75% and a specificity of nearly 100%. Patients with APLA and one major clinical criterion are considered to have APLA syndrome. Primary APLA syndrome refers to the syndrome occurring outside the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus.38 In women with APLA, there is a high incidence of pregnancy complications. Among women with a history of recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive losses of pregnancy), 15% have persistently positive test results for APLA and a rate of fetal loss of 90% when no specific treatment is given during pregnancy. Twenty-five percent of successful pregnancies are delivered prematurely. Other potential complications of pregnancy include preeclampsia, placental insufficiency, fetal growth impairment, preterm birth, maternal thrombosis (including stroke), and complications of treatment.38,39
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

paragraphs.text: The adverse effect of APLA syndrome on pregnancy is most likely associated with abnormal placental function. Studies
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

paragraphs.text: have shown abnormalities in the decidual spiral arteries, narrowing of the spiral arterioles, intimal thickening, acute atherosis, and fibrinoid necrosis in cases of fetal loss associated with APLA syndrome.38,39 Other studies have found extensive placental necrosis, infarction, and thrombosis related to the procoagulant activity of APLAs in inducing adhesion molecules, platelet activation, and aggregation factors and the inhibition of key anticoagulant factors (see Chapter 25). Data demonstrate a positive correlation between the amounts of antibodies and adverse pregnancy outcomes.40
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

paragraphs.text: The combination of aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin is the acceptable treatment for decreasing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcome in patients with APLA syndrome. Hydroxychloroquine improves pregnancy outcomes among patients with lupus. Other treatment options include corticosteroids and IVIG, mostly to treat other lupus symptoms. Data support second-line treatments with azathioprine and rituximab for mainly refractory thrombocytopenia, lupus nephritis, or interstitial lung disease. No major congenital abnormalities or defects were described, although the data are limited. See Table 19.2.
paragraphs.heading: Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

paragraphs.text: Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disease affecting twice as many women as men, and it usually affects women in their third decade of life. The symptoms include weakness and fatigue of the skeletal muscles of the face and extremities. The diagnosis, which is beyond the scope of this chapter, involves a comprehensive neurologic workup based on clinical history and signs, improvement with anticholinesterase injection (edrophonium), determination of serum anti–acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody titers by radioimmunoassay, and electromyography.
paragraphs.heading: Myasthenia Gravis

paragraphs.text: In 90% of patients with MG, autoantibodies (usually IgG) against human AChRs are detected. The antibodies interfere with impulse conduction across neuromuscular junctions by decreasing the number of available AChRs there. Because MG typically affects women during reproductive years, the potential for exacerbation, respiratory failure, adverse drug response, crisis, and death during pregnancy is of great concern. MG has a variable and unpredictable course during pregnancy, including exacerbation, crisis, and remission.41 In
paragraphs.heading: Myasthenia Gravis

paragraphs.text: one study, 17% of asymptomatic patients with MG who were not receiving therapy before conception had a relapse; among patients receiving therapy, MG symptoms improved in 39%, remained unchanged in 42%, and deteriorated in 19% of the pregnancies. MG symptoms worsened after delivery in 28% of the pregnancies.42 In another study, MG symptoms deteriorated in 15% of the pregnancies, and a further 16% deteriorated during the puerperium.43
paragraphs.heading: Myasthenia Gravis

paragraphs.text: Therapy is based on anticholinesterase medications and plasmapheresis during an MG crisis. Other medications often have adverse effects on the disease, resulting in a long list of drugs that should be avoided in these patients. Plasmapheresis can be performed during pregnancy but may be associated with preterm birth. Of special concern are cesarean delivery and the hazards of anesthesia, which might prove very stressful for these patients. Some complications of MG in the form of exacerbation should be anticipated during pregnancy, including anxiety and physiologic stress of pregnancy (mainly present as hypoventilation), infection, a prolonged second stage at delivery (because the patient may become exhausted and be unable to push), and the contraindication to using magnesium sulfate in patients with preeclampsia.
paragraphs.heading: Myasthenia Gravis

paragraphs.text: Neonatal risks of MG include neonatal MG, prematurity, malformation, and death. Neonatal MG occurs in 10% to 20% of infants born to mothers with MG and is caused by the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins from mother to infant. Specific antibodies and probably specific genetic predisposition influence the rate and severity of neonatal MG.44 There is no correlation between MG severity and neonatal MG, and there is no correlation between maternal anti-AChR antibody titers and the occurrence of neonatal MG. This discrepancy is partially explained in neonatal MG by the protective role of α-fetoprotein, which inhibits the binding of MG antibody to its receptor.
paragraphs.heading: Myasthenia Gravis

paragraphs.text: The infant’s symptoms are generally manifested by the third day of life in the form of respiratory distress and inadequate suck, which may gradually subside over 1 to 4 weeks. Rarely, the disease becomes permanent when there is irreversible destruction of AChR by the maternal antibodies or when there is production of antibodies by the infant. Analysis of data collected from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway comparing 127 births by women with MG with 1.9 million births by women without MG showed that women with MG had a higher rate of complications at delivery. In particular, the risk for preterm rupture of membranes was threefold higher in the MG group. Interventions during birth were also significantly increased, and the rate of cesarean section was twice that of the general population. Five children (3.9%) born to mothers with MG had severe anomalies, and three of them died.45 Maternal thymectomy prior to conception is controversial and is unlikely to result in maternal remission of MG. A retrospective analysis of data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway found a protective effect of thymectomy against neonatal MG. Neonates of mothers with MG who had undergone thymectomy were less likely to develop neonatal MG than those born to mothers without thymectomy

paragraphs.text: Pemphigoid gestationis (formerly referred to as herpes gestationis) is a rare autoimmune skin disease of pregnancy, occurring in less than 1 in about 50,000 pregnancies. During pregnancy, IgG autoantibodies are produced against an important element in epidermal-dermal adhesion—the bullous pemphigoid antigen 2 (BPAg2; also known as BP180). It is assumed that these autoantibodies bind complement to the basement membrane of the epidermis and activate an immunodermatologic reaction that is responsible for the development of subepidermal vesiculae and bullae.47,48 Pemphigoid gestationis is sometimes associated with other autoimmune diseases, and it seems that all these conditions have in common a relationship to HLA-B8 and HLA-DR3. Although pemphigoid gestationis most commonly manifests during the second and third trimesters, in 25% of the cases it develops during the puerperium. There are reported cases of persistent herpes pemphigoid gestationis, but usually the disease spontaneously regresses after birth.49
paragraphs.heading: Pemphigoid Gestationis

paragraphs.text: Affected women usually present with inexorable pruritus associated with erythematous urticarial patches and plaques, which are typically located around the navel. The skin lesions may progress to tense vesicles and blisters, which spread peripherally. The face, palms, soles, and mucous membranes are usually unaffected. Although the symptoms usually wane toward the end of pregnancy, peripartum exacerbations do exist. Pemphigoid gestationis may recur in subsequent pregnancies, and it may recur with menses and oral contraception.
paragraphs.heading: Pemphigoid Gestationis

paragraphs.text: The diagnosis is usually reached by collaboration between the attending obstetrician and an immunodermatologist. Treatment is directed toward alleviation of itching and suppression of blistering. Lukewarm baths or compresses may reduce the irritation; antihistamines can help to reduce pruritus. Corticosteroids (local, intralesional, or systemic) remain the primary therapeutic means. Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, dapsone, and IVIG have also been effective. Rituximab (US Food and Drug Administration Pregnancy Risk Category C), is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that exerts its effects in pemphigus through depletion of B cells, which are responsible for the production of antidesmoglein autoantibodies. It may cross the placenta, but no congenital anomalies or fetal damage have been reported so far, although the data are limited.50–53
paragraphs.heading: Pemphigoid Gestationis

paragraphs.text: Pemphigoid gestationis is associated with a greater incidence of premature birth and neonates who are small for gestational age. The infants of affected mothers may rarely have transient cutaneous manifestations, which disappear along with the clearance of maternal autoantibodies. Blistering may increase the risk, however, for superimposed infection, thermoregulatory problems, and fluid and electrolyte imbalance. The attending neonatologist should also be aware of the medications received by the mother.54

### TAL BIRON-SHENTAL AND CALANIT HERSHKOVICH-SHPOREN

### Placental Transfer: General Remarks

The maternal-fetal interface is quite efficient in its selective exclusion of substances during the transport process from the maternal to the fetal circulation. At the same time, the placenta selectively transfers other substances, a process that is facilitated by the proximity of the respective maternal-fetal vascular systems within the placental cotyledons. Although there is no mixing of the maternal and fetal blood, the placental barrier is not impermeable, and small amounts of fetal blood, including fetal cells, gain access to the maternal circulation in most pregnancies through breaks in the fetal-maternal interface. When fetal blood cells are recognized as antigens by the maternal immunologic system, they may provoke an immune response and the production of immunoglobulins. This mechanism occurs in only a few pregnancies and is the basis of incompatibility disorders (see Chapter 22), whereby exogenous antigens such as fetal cells or incompatible blood sensitize the maternal immune system. The maternal antibodies, which are produced as a response to sensitization, cross the placenta and may destroy fetal cells.1,2 Generally, the mother is disease free, and the diagnosis is reached usually after the delivery of an affected infant and in some cases by sonographic findings.

A second type of maternal antibody that crosses the placenta and affects the fetus may arise from sensitization of the mother’s immune system by her endogenous antigens, with the resultant production of autoantibodies. The mother with autoantibodies has an autoimmune disorder, and the diagnosis of the maternal disease usually precedes the diagnosis of the fetal or neonatal complication.

These generalizations describe immune processes that may affect the fetus or neonate. Although the maternal immune system may produce a wide range of immunoglobulins, only maternal antibodies of the immunoglobulin G (IgG) class (but not IgM or IgA) can cross the placental barrier. The common denominators of such disorders are the production of IgG in the maternal compartment, the transfer of IgG through the placenta, and the effects of these

352

antibodies in the fetal compartment or neonate. Maternal IgG antibodies are also transferred to the newborns through breast feeding and may cause autoimmunity pathologies.3–5 This chapter discusses examples of such disorders.

### Fetal Thrombocytopenia

Box 19.1 lists the immunologic etiologies of fetal and consequently neonatal thrombocytopenia. The most significant pathologies are neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia and immune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Although the two conditions have some similarities, they are distinct diseases, each with a different underlying pathogenesis (Table 19.1) (see Chapter 80).

### Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura

ITP in adults is often a chronic disease mediated by autoantibodies directed against cell surface components (glycoproteins) of platelets (IIb/IIIa or Ib/IX). Thrombocytopenia occurs when the platelet-antibody complexes are destroyed by the reticuloendothelial system. A low platelet count raises suspicion for ITP, but the diagnosis is reached after exclusion of other causes of thrombocytopenia by history, physical examination, blood count, peripheral blood smear, and autoimmune profile.6–8 A spuriously low platelet count should be evaluated by examining a blood smear to exclude

### Fetal and Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia

Fetal and neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (FNAIT) is a rare but serious condition associated with significant fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. The pathogenesis is similar to Rh disease. A mother with antigen-negative platelets is sensitized by antigen-positive fetal platelets gaining access to the maternal circulation via breaches in the placental barrier. As a result, the mother produces antiplatelet antibodies, and these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy the fetal platelets. In contrast to Rh disease, 50% of FNAIT cases occur during the first pregnancy of couples at risk. This difference is explained by the higher immunogenicity of the platelet antigen and the smaller size of the platelets, which may facilitate their fetomaternal transfusion.

Of the several types of platelet antigens, the human platelet antigen 1a (HPA-1a) is involved in 80% to 90% of FNAIT cases among Caucasians, and HPA-5b is responsible for a further 5% to 15% of the cases. Among people of color (e.g., Asians), HPA-1a incompatibility is a rare cause of FNAIT, and other alloantigens (e.g., HPA-4b) are implicated. The fetus acquires the antigen from the father. When the father is heterozygous, 50% of the fetuses would be affected, whereas all fetuses of a homozygous father would be HPA positive.16,17 The prevalence of FNAIT is 1 case per 1000 deliveries. Fetomaternal platelet incompatibility is much more frequent. The discrepancy is explained by the facilitating role of certain human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types that are associated with the development of FNAIT. HLA-DR3 is associated with a 10- to 30-fold risk for HPA- 1a antibody production.

In the usual scenario, an asymptomatic woman delivers an otherwise normal infant in an otherwise uncomplicated birth. Most neonates are asymptomatic, and the thrombocytopenia is detected by a blood count performed for other perinatal causes. In some cases, neonates present with generalized petechiae, hemorrhage into abdominal viscera, excessive bleeding after venipuncture or circumcision, or, in extreme cases, abnormal neurologic manifestations secondary to ICH. The platelet count commonly decreases further during the first week after birth. Less common presentation is an intrauterine sonographic diagnosis of fetal ICH, found to be secondary to fetal thrombocytopenia caused by FNAIT.18,19

The diagnosis of FNAIT involves typing platelet antigens in the newborn and in the parents to show that the mother lacks a platelet antigen that is present on the platelets of the father and the neonate. A more sophisticated test is to establish the existence of the antiplatelet antibody in the mother’s serum that is directed against a platelet antigen in

the father. Testing the infant is generally unnecessary if the father is available for testing. HPA genotyping is available as a routine laboratory technique and can be used to identify HPA incompatibilities between mother and child. Universal screening is not recommended by any professional organization due to the low prevalence of FNAIT. However, it is possible to accurately screen for HPA-1a, which causes 75% of FNAIT cases.20–22

### Management of the Neonate

In suspected cases of FNAIT, treatment should be started on the basis of the clinical diagnosis without waiting for the results of the immunologic workup. Management depends on the gestational age of the infant, the severity of the thrombocytopenia, the presence of bleeding, and the presence of additional risk factors for bleeding. Treatment is based on transfusion of random-donor, ABO-compatible and Rh-compatible, and HPA-1a-negative platelets (preferably with HPA-5b-negative platelets, as well) in neonates with severe thrombocytopenia. This transfusion is compatible in approximately 90% of cases of FNAIT.22 When random-donor platelets are unavailable, washed maternal platelets can be administered. HPA-incompatible platelets should be used only if compatible ones are unavailable; they can be combined with IVIG treatment to achieve a transient increase in the platelet count until IVIG becomes effective.20

High-dose IVIG, 1 g/kg per day for 2 days or 0.5 g/kg per day for 4 days, is also effective in increasing the platelet count in most cases, although the increase may be delayed for 1 or 2 days.9 Corticosteroids were used in the past but have become less popular since the availability of IVIG. In any case, the neonatal platelet count should be closely monitored during the first days of life.

### Management of a Subsequent Pregnancy

When the diagnosis of alloimmune thrombocytopenia is established, parents should be counseled regarding risks and management of future pregnancies. The recurrence rate of FNAIT in a subsequent pregnancy is greater than 90%, and the risk for ICH is the same or greater than in the previous pregnancy. There are conflicting data regarding increased severity of FNAIT in subsequent pregnancies.23

HPA-1a alloimmunization tends to cause a more significant disease compared to other antibodies. Low and stable maternal levels of HPA-1a during the pregnancy are correlated with a low risk of FNAIT development.24 Fetal ICH in previous pregnancies increase the risk of recurrence, which tends to be in earlier gestational weeks. Administration of IVIG therapy during the pregnancy is considered protective against FNAIT.

The risk for antenatal ICH in the fetus with alloimmune thrombocytopenia is substantial enough to warrant intervention by giving the mother weekly infusions of high-dose IVIG with or without corticosteroids. Antenatal therapy is aimed at increasing the number of fetal platelets regardless of the presence of a risk factor.

If the father is heterozygous, the status of the fetus is unknown. In some places, a noninvasive evaluation of fetal typing through maternal blood is available. Direct assessment of fetal platelets via PUBS or via genotyping cells in the amniotic fluid may be performed. The timing of the procedure and the risk involved are matters of debate. Failure to treat carries the risk for intrauterine ICH, which is expected to occur in 30% of cases, with 10% of affected newborns dying and 20% experiencing neurologic sequelae secondary to ICH. PUBS has a high risk for miscarriage or fetal death. The operator must be prepared to transfuse platelets if the results show a dangerously low platelet count. If the infant is found to be HPA positive or the father is homozygous for the allele, there is a choice between serial platelet transfusions and IVIG administered to the mother. Amniocentesis is performed mainly to exclude the presence of platelet antigens and thus to avoid unnecessary interventions.25-27

Serial intrauterine platelet transfusions carry the risk of a single PUBS multiplied by the number of procedures. Because the survival of transfused thrombocytes is short, performing serial intrauterine transfusions requires repeating the procedure every week or 10 days. In a study of the fetal loss rate in FNAIT managed by serial platelet transfusions, the authors found two perinatal losses in 12 pregnancies managed by a total of 84 platelet transfusions. One loss was procedure related and resulted from exsanguination despite platelet transfusion. The procedure-related fetal loss rate was 1.2% per procedure but 8.3% per pregnancy. The authors calculated a cumulative risk for serial weekly transfusions of approximately 6% per pregnancy, indicating the need to develop less invasive approaches.28

The invasive procedure is used less often now than previously; this may be the result of favorable outcomes related to maternal

treatment with high-dose IVIG (1 g/kg/wk). The beneficial effect of megadose IVIG is presumably mediated by masking the antigenic effect of fetal platelets, reducing the production of antiplatelet antibodies. IVIG also stabilizes endothelial cells and reduces the incidence of ICH even when the fetal platelet count remains low. It is debatable whether corticosteroids should be added to the IVIG management protocol.20,21,29

A European collaborative study of the antenatal management of FNAIT attempted to determine whether the severity of the disease in the current pregnancy could be predicted from the history of FNAIT in previous pregnancies and to assess the effects of different types of antenatal intervention. The study enrolled 56 women who had had a prior infant affected by FNAIT due to HPA-1a alloimmunization. The authors found that fetuses with a sibling history of antenatal ICH or severe thrombocytopenia (a platelet count of <20,000/μL) had significantly lower pretreatment platelet counts than fetuses whose siblings had less severe thrombocytopenia or postnatal ICH. Maternal therapy resulted in a platelet count exceeding 50,000/μL in 67% of cases. None of the fetuses managed by serial platelet intrauterine transfusions had ICH after treatment. Several serious complications of PUBS arose, however. The results of this study suggest that the start of therapy can be stratified on the basis of the sibling history of FNAIT and support the use of maternal therapy as first-line treatment.10

Some patients who receive IVIG do not respond. Nonresponders cannot be recognized without PUBS, however. When PUBS is planned to assess the effectiveness of therapy, the preparation for intrauterine platelet transfusion should be similar to the procedure used when PUBS is performed to diagnose FNAIT in a case with a heterozygous father (i.e., when the risk of an affected fetus is 50%). Nonresponders may be treated with either serial intrauterine platelet transfusions or steroids added to IVIG. It has been suggested that such assessment of treatment is unnecessary in patients who previously responded to IVIG therapy.

Alloimmune thrombocytopenia may also result from fetomaternal HLA mismatch. The meaning and treatment of this rare situation are controversial.

Most patients are delivered by a term planned cesarean delivery. For patients who desire a vaginal delivery, a fetal platelet count is suggested for safety evaluation of a vaginal delivery. For patients with prior pregnancies with FNAIT, avoiding an affected fetus may be achieved by preimplantation genetic testing and an in vitro fertilization.21,30

Anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are specific for systemic lupus erythematosus. In this chapter, the maternal manifestations of these autoimmune diseases are not discussed; the focus is on neonatal lupus—a model of passively acquired autoimmunity—and the effects of the ANAs anti-Ro and anti-La.

Neonatal lupus is caused by transplacental passage of maternal autoantibodies. It is rare, as only about 1% of infants with maternal ANAs develop neonatal lupus. The infant may present with cardiac, dermatologic, hepatic, and hematologic manifestations. In children with neonatal lupus, there is commonly involvement of only one or two organ systems. The skin lesions on the face and scalp, often in a distinctive periorbital distribution, may be present at birth but usually develop within the first few weeks of life and tend to resolve in a few weeks or months without scarring.31 Fetal heart block typically begins during the second or third trimester of pregnancy. In some instances, this begins as first- or second-degree heart block and progresses to third-degree heart block. Complete heart block seems to be irreversible and may be combined with cardiomyopathy (see Chapter 78). Hepatobiliary complications (10% of cases) may be manifested as liver failure occurring at birth or in utero, transient conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, or transient transaminase elevations occurring in infancy. Thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or anemia occurs in about 10% of affected infants. The noncardiac manifestations are transient and tend to resolve within months after birth. A case of neonatal lupus affecting both twins has been described.32

Mothers of children with neonatal lupus may have ANA-related connective tissue disease (e.g., systemic lupus

erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, undifferentiated autoimmune syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis). The recurrence rate of neonatal lupus for a mother with anti-Ro autoantibodies, which are present in almost 95% of patients, is approximately 25%. IgG autoantibodies are found alone or in combination and are directed against Ro (SSA), La (SSB), or U1-RNA (U1-RNP) antigens, and their presence increases the risk for neonatal lupus erythematosus.

Anti-Ro and anti-La autoantibodies recognize cardiac adrenoceptors and muscarinic receptors, and this recognition may explain the cardiac arrhythmia associated with these ANAs. Maternal anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and complement components are deposited in fetal heart tissues, leading to inflammation, calcification, necrosis, and fibrosis of the conducting tissue (and, in some cases, of the surrounding myocardium).33 The postinflammation fibrotic response to injury is quite rapid and, in most cases, irreversible. The process by which maternal anti-Ro or anti-La antibodies begin and propagate inflammation that leads to scarring of the atrioventricular node is not entirely clear. It has been proposed that the process begins with apoptosis of cardiocytes, resulting in translocation of Ro or La antigens and subsequent surface binding by maternal ANAs. This leads to a phagocytosis-mediated scarring process.33 In addition, the anti-Ro antibodies have been shown to have arrhythmogenic activity through inhibition of calcium flux across cell membranes.34 Animal models suggest that reactivity to the p200 region of the Ro52 protein and antibody targeting of L-type calcium channels may be associated in the developing cardiac neonatal lupus.35 In vitro, the β2-glycoprotein I seems to prevent anti-Ro binding to apoptotic cells, the urokinase-plasminogen activator/receptor system seems to activate transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), and endothelin-1 secretion by macrophages seems to mediate tissue injury.35 It also appears that fetal major histocompatibility complex is involved in the pathogenesis.35 Interestingly, it was demonstrated that mothers of children with neonatal lupus accumulate genetic risk factors preferentially from the neonatal lupus child’s grandparents.35

The cardiac rhythm disorders increase the risk for fetal congestive heart failure and point to the most important intervention during pregnancy: close follow-up with echocardiography and ultrasonography. Echocardiography can show the conduction defect and estimate the cardiac function.

About 10% of fetuses with congenital heart block are born with hydrops fetalis and congestive heart failure, and their prognosis is poor (see Chapter 22). Retrospective studies addressed the role of fluorinated steroids, IVIG, and hydroxychloroquine for prevention and treatment.35 Intrauterine treatment with maternal corticosteroids may decrease the pericardial effusion or improve the symptoms of heart failure. If first- or second-degree heart block is detected, oral dexamethasone, 4 mg daily, is recommended. The treatment is controversial because some of those blocks may resolve spontaneously, and dexamethasone treatment crosses placentas and may cause abortion, oligohydramnios, and abnormal fetal growth along with either maternal

### Fetal-Neonatal Consequences of Maternal Antiphospholipid Antibodies

Phospholipids are involved in facilitating the coagulation cascade. Antiphospholipid antibodies (APLAs) are autoantibodies against phospholipids or against plasma proteins bound to phospholipids. The most common subgroups involved in disease states are anticardiolipin antibodies, lupus anticoagulant antibodies, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies. The hypercoagulability function of these antibodies is epitomized by the fact that they cause “bleeding in the test tube but clotting in the body,” referring to their involvement in pathologic clotting. APLAs promote clotting in arteries and veins (i.e., thrombophilia) by activation of endothelial cells, via oxidantmediated injury to endothelium, and by modulating the regulatory function of coagulation proteins.

It is common practice to use clinical and laboratory criteria for the diagnosis of APLA syndrome. According to the Sapporo criteria, patients are required to have either vascular thrombosis (venous or arterial, including neurologic disease) or fetal loss and to show evidence of APLA either by the detection of anticardiolipin antibodies or by a positive test for lupus anticoagulant antibodies. At present, one should look for lupus anticoagulant, APLA, and anti-β2-glycoprotein I. To differentiate between persistent autoantibody response and transient responses from other causes, APLA must be detected on at least two occasions 12 weeks apart. These classification criteria are reported to have a sensitivity of greater than 75% and a specificity of nearly 100%. Patients with APLA and one major clinical criterion are considered to have APLA syndrome. Primary APLA syndrome refers to the syndrome occurring outside the setting of systemic lupus erythematosus.38 In women with APLA, there is a high incidence of pregnancy complications. Among women with a history of recurrent miscarriage (three or more consecutive losses of pregnancy), 15% have persistently positive test results for APLA and a rate of fetal loss of 90% when no specific treatment is given during pregnancy. Twenty-five percent of successful pregnancies are delivered prematurely. Other potential complications of pregnancy include preeclampsia, placental insufficiency, fetal growth impairment, preterm birth, maternal thrombosis (including stroke), and complications of treatment.38,39

The adverse effect of APLA syndrome on pregnancy is most likely associated with abnormal placental function. Studies

have shown abnormalities in the decidual spiral arteries, narrowing of the spiral arterioles, intimal thickening, acute atherosis, and fibrinoid necrosis in cases of fetal loss associated with APLA syndrome.38,39 Other studies have found extensive placental necrosis, infarction, and thrombosis related to the procoagulant activity of APLAs in inducing adhesion molecules, platelet activation, and aggregation factors and the inhibition of key anticoagulant factors (see Chapter 25). Data demonstrate a positive correlation between the amounts of antibodies and adverse pregnancy outcomes.40

The combination of aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin is the acceptable treatment for decreasing the risk of adverse pregnancy outcome in patients with APLA syndrome. Hydroxychloroquine improves pregnancy outcomes among patients with lupus. Other treatment options include corticosteroids and IVIG, mostly to treat other lupus symptoms. Data support second-line treatments with azathioprine and rituximab for mainly refractory thrombocytopenia, lupus nephritis, or interstitial lung disease. No major congenital abnormalities or defects were described, although the data are limited. See Table 19.2.

### Myasthenia Gravis

Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune neuromuscular disease affecting twice as many women as men, and it usually affects women in their third decade of life. The symptoms include weakness and fatigue of the skeletal muscles of the face and extremities. The diagnosis, which is beyond the scope of this chapter, involves a comprehensive neurologic workup based on clinical history and signs, improvement with anticholinesterase injection (edrophonium), determination of serum anti–acetylcholine receptor (AChR) antibody titers by radioimmunoassay, and electromyography.

In 90% of patients with MG, autoantibodies (usually IgG) against human AChRs are detected. The antibodies interfere with impulse conduction across neuromuscular junctions by decreasing the number of available AChRs there. Because MG typically affects women during reproductive years, the potential for exacerbation, respiratory failure, adverse drug response, crisis, and death during pregnancy is of great concern. MG has a variable and unpredictable course during pregnancy, including exacerbation, crisis, and remission.41 In

Neonatal risks of MG include neonatal MG, prematurity, malformation, and death. Neonatal MG occurs in 10% to 20% of infants born to mothers with MG and is caused by the transplacental transport of immunoglobulins from mother to infant. Specific antibodies and probably specific genetic predisposition influence the rate and severity of neonatal MG.44 There is no correlation between MG severity and neonatal MG, and there is no correlation between maternal anti-AChR antibody titers and the occurrence of neonatal MG. This discrepancy is partially explained in neonatal MG by the protective role of α-fetoprotein, which inhibits the binding of MG antibody to its receptor.

The infant’s symptoms are generally manifested by the third day of life in the form of respiratory distress and inadequate suck, which may gradually subside over 1 to 4 weeks. Rarely, the disease becomes permanent when there is irreversible destruction of AChR by the maternal antibodies or when there is production of antibodies by the infant. Analysis of data collected from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway comparing 127 births by women with MG with 1.9 million births by women without MG showed that women with MG had a higher rate of complications at delivery. In particular, the risk for preterm rupture of membranes was threefold higher in the MG group. Interventions during birth were also significantly increased, and the rate of cesarean section was twice that of the general population. Five children (3.9%) born to mothers with MG had severe anomalies, and three of them died.45 Maternal thymectomy prior to conception is controversial and is unlikely to result in maternal remission of MG. A retrospective analysis of data from the Medical Birth Registry of Norway found a protective effect of thymectomy against neonatal MG. Neonates of mothers with MG who had undergone thymectomy were less likely to develop neonatal MG than those born to mothers without thymectomy

### Pemphigoid Gestationis

Pemphigoid gestationis (formerly referred to as herpes gestationis) is a rare autoimmune skin disease of pregnancy, occurring in less than 1 in about 50,000 pregnancies. During pregnancy, IgG autoantibodies are produced against an important element in epidermal-dermal adhesion—the bullous pemphigoid antigen 2 (BPAg2; also known as BP180). It is assumed that these autoantibodies bind complement to the basement membrane of the epidermis and activate an immunodermatologic reaction that is responsible for the development of subepidermal vesiculae and bullae.47,48 Pemphigoid gestationis is sometimes associated with other autoimmune diseases, and it seems that all these conditions have in common a relationship to HLA-B8 and HLA-DR3. Although pemphigoid gestationis most commonly manifests during the second and third trimesters, in 25% of the cases it develops during the puerperium. There are reported cases of persistent herpes pemphigoid gestationis, but usually the disease spontaneously regresses after birth.49

Affected women usually present with inexorable pruritus associated with erythematous urticarial patches and plaques, which are typically located around the navel. The skin lesions may progress to tense vesicles and blisters, which spread peripherally. The face, palms, soles, and mucous membranes are usually unaffected. Although the symptoms usually wane toward the end of pregnancy, peripartum exacerbations do exist. Pemphigoid gestationis may recur in subsequent pregnancies, and it may recur with menses and oral contraception.

The diagnosis is usually reached by collaboration between the attending obstetrician and an immunodermatologist. Treatment is directed toward alleviation of itching and suppression of blistering. Lukewarm baths or compresses may reduce the irritation; antihistamines can help to reduce pruritus. Corticosteroids (local, intralesional, or systemic) remain the primary therapeutic means. Immunosuppressants such as azathioprine, cyclosporine, dapsone, and IVIG have also been effective. Rituximab (US Food and Drug Administration Pregnancy Risk Category C), is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that exerts its effects in pemphigus through depletion of B cells, which are responsible for the production of antidesmoglein autoantibodies. It may cross the placenta, but no congenital anomalies or fetal damage have been reported so far, although the data are limited.50–53

Pemphigoid gestationis is associated with a greater incidence of premature birth and neonates who are small for gestational age. The infants of affected mothers may rarely have transient cutaneous manifestations, which disappear along with the clearance of maternal autoantibodies. Blistering may increase the risk, however, for superimposed infection, thermoregulatory problems, and fluid and electrolyte imbalance. The attending neonatologist should also be aware of the medications received by the mother.54
